question.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Even Power
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13930904/assets/67b77d2d3798e87593c7dddeea93603fff36d9153f53248cc2dab295f4879321.png)

The figure above shows the graph of $f(x).$ Find ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{f(x)}.$
question.worked_solution:
Applying the product rule and the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }({x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{f(x)}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot ({lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{f(x)}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{({lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x))}\end{aligned}
$$

From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x)=3.$ Therefore, the above becomes:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{2}$ is an upward parabola, so

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}=\infty .
$$

Multiplication by the positive constant $\frac{1}{3}$ does not change the sign of the limit. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2})={lim}_{x\to -\infty }({x}^{2})=\infty .\end{aligned}
$$
